newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao given ultimatum to quit party post.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao given ultimatum to quit party post.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao faced an ultimatum to quit his last party post on Thursday as Congress stepped up efforts to rebuild after its worst ever electoral defeat.
Congress party president Sitaram Kesri sent a letter late on Wednesday telling Rao to step down from his influential post as head of the party's parliamentary bloc by 4 p.m. (1030 GMT) on Thursday.
Kesri's letter followed an unprecedented resolution by leaders of the parliamentary delegation demanding that Rao give up his post for the sake of party unity.

Rao, who spearheaded India's move away from socialist economic controls to open markets, led the country from 1991 until last May when the 111-year-old Congress suffered its worst ever defeat in general elections.
The 75-year-old politician has been charged in three separate corruption cases. He denies any wrongdoing in the cases which are before trial judges.
The spate of allegations forced him to step down as Congress president in September and has undercut his authority.
Still, party insiders said Rao might defy the ultimatum and force a showdown between his dwindling forces and the new leadership under Kesri, an apostle of Mahatma Gandhi.

"It is clear he is not going to resign," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil told Reuters. He said the Congress Parliamentary Party, comprising 229 lawmakers in both houses of parliament, might have to take a vote, or the party could force out Rao.
"We may have to expel him," Gadgil said.

The campaign to drive Rao from the last pedestal of power was part of a broader effort to revive Congress's flagging fortunes, intimately tied to Rao's wily manoeuvring during his last years in power and, more recently, his legal woes.
"The Congress paid a heavy price at the hustings for his shortsighted power games," The Tribune newspaper said.
The Asian Age newspaper said "a large number of Congressmen...are silently hoping that with his departure, the taint of corruption that has dogged the party in recent times will also go".
The prospect of a rejuvenated Congress has sent tremors through Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 13-party centre-left United Front coalition.
The government depends on the support of Congress, with control over 142 deputies in the 545-member lower house of parliament, to survive.
Preoccupied with its own internal problems, Congress has to date been a mild critic of Deve Gowda's minority government.
United Front leaders believe "the ouster of Mr Rao will leave them facing a Congress which may not be content with playing the role of silent supporter", the Economic Times said.

"The United Front government is bound to feel rather uneasy about the change because Mr Kesri has been less enthusiastic about continuing Congress support for Mr Deve Gowda than Mr Rao," The Asian Age said.
But Rao's departure could lead to a tussle among Congress heavyweights for control of the party's parliamentary bloc, giving the United Front some breathing room, analysts said.

Most Congress leaders, smarting from the recent electoral debacle, are not yet ready for mid-term polls but might explore possible alliances with a view to building a new govering coalition, they said.
